hints: Look very carefully at where each inhibitor is sitting. Is inhibitor X inside the active site, while inhibitor Y is attached somewhere else on the enzyme?
Remember the rule: binding directly in the active site to block the substrate is competitive, while binding elsewhere and changing the shape of the active site is non-competitive.
walkthrough:
**Look at inhibitor X**

Inhibitor X is drawn sitting right inside the labelled active site. It is physically occupying the space where the substrate would normally fit.

This is the classic picture of blocking the active site directly.

**Look at inhibitor Y**

Inhibitor Y is attached to a different part of the enzyme, away from the active site. The diagram even shows a dashed outline labelled change in the shape of the active site.

So Y is not blocking the site, it is changing its shape from a distance.

**Match to the inhibition types**

Competitive inhibitor = similar shape to substrate, fits into active site, competes for the space.

Non-competitive inhibitor = binds at another site, alters the 3D shape of the active site so substrate no longer fits.

Therefore X is competitive and Y is non-competitive, which is row B.

options.A: Y cannot be competitive because it does not enter the active site, it binds elsewhere and changes the active site shape.
options.B: X sits in the active site so it is competitive, Y binds elsewhere and changes active site shape so it is non-competitive.
options.C: This is the wrong way round. X is in the active site, not elsewhere, so X is not non-competitive.
options.D: X cannot be non-competitive because it binds directly inside the active site with no change in shape shown.
